title: Due Care, Due Diligence, and the Prudent Man Rule
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 7: Security Operations: Due Care, Due Diligence, and the Prudent Man Rule.

items: Due Care — taking reasonable steps to protect assets; "doing the right thing" (actions)
Due Diligence — researching and understanding risks before making decisions; "doing homework" (investigation)
Prudent Man Rule — a senior executive must take personal responsibility for ensuring due care; originated from the U.S. Federal Sentencing Guidelines (1991)
Gross Negligence — failure to exercise even basic care; e.g., failing to apply critical security patches for months
A company that fails to implement reasonable security (e.g., no SSL for financial transactions) is not practicing due care

blocks.text: From Shon Harris: "Many times due diligence (data gathering) has to be performed so that proper due care (prudent actions) can take place." If a company does not implement SSL for account transactions, it is not practicing due care. The U.S. Federal Sentencing Guidelines of 1991 formalized the Prudent Man Rule, requiring senior executives to take personal responsibility for ensuring due care in protecting organizational assets. This directly applies to security operations: a manager who knows about a critical vulnerability but fails to patch it could be found grossly negligent. Operational Due Care Examples:

items: Patching systems within a reasonable timeframe → due care
Failing to patch a known critical vulnerability for 6+ months → gross negligence
Conducting a risk assessment before selecting a cloud provider → due diligence
Implementing security controls based on risk assessment findings → due care

blocks.text: Manager Mindset: On the CISSP exam, the "correct" answer often involves the manager ensuring due diligence is performed (understanding risks) and due care is exercised (taking action). Failing to do either can result in legal liability. ⚠️ Exam Trap: Due diligence = research/investigation. Due care = action/implementation. The Prudent Man Rule holds executives personally responsible. Gross negligence is the failure to exercise basic care — it can result in both civil and criminal penalties.
